heading: Summary
note: The one-page Summary: the task of building a repeater network (2), the constructive approach taken (3), the synthetic population data used for testing (4), and what the colour-gradient plots show (5). Stored count 4 agrees.

heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background)
note: The introduction: the goal of an extendible, flexible algorithm (9), VHF propagation in the 145-148 MHz band (10), the range limit that makes repeaters necessary (11), and the channel offsets and frequency pairs that let a repeater receive and retransmit (12-13). Stored count 7 against four printed units.

heading: 1.2 The Problem
note: The problem statement itself: wide-area broadcast comes at a cost in capacity (14), and the task is the minimum number of repeaters serving a given population without blocking (15). Stored count 6 against two printed units; the stored bucket folds the whole of 1 Background in with it.

heading: 2 Assumptions
note: Nine assumptions, printed as First through Finally: instantaneous propagation, nine-mile range, interference and licensing codes, minimum spacing, equal load per user, a US setting, and the call distribution. Block 17-18 carries the assumption list's opening and the sentence that they are reasonable. Stored count 12 against ten printed units.

heading: 3 Metric (3.1 Measuring Transmission Capacity)
note: The metric and its simulation: accommodation defined as the fraction of users served (29-30), requests that reach an uncovered user counted as unfulfilled (31-32), and the timestep simulation that queues transmissions and counts what interference blocks (33-49, one pseudocode listing). Stored count 4 against three printed units.

heading: 3.2 Generating Requests and 3.3 Measuring Overall Quality
note: How the request stream is synthesised: the difficulty of choosing a request model (50), the per-user request assignment with its tower-count parameter (51), and the overall-quality combination of coverage and capacity (52). Stored count 5 against three printed units.

heading: 4 Approach (4.1 Modeling Population Density, 4.2 Linking Strategies)
note: The model's inputs and its linking vocabulary: Gaussian population densities with the chosen sigma (54-56), Figure 1's five distributions (57-62), two-way frequency offset pairs (63-70), the staggered chain idea and its bi-directional extension (71-72). Blocks 58-61 are the figure panels and 65-69 the five frequency pairs. Stored count 8 against ten printed units.

heading: 4.3 Naive Approach
note: The naive baseline and why it fails: blanket 9-mile placement (73-74), the network it produces (75), and the feedback problem that rules it out (76). Stored label error-analysis is outside the fourteen-value vocabulary and is kept verbatim. Stored count 5 against four printed units.

heading: 4.4 Implementing Privacy Lines to Reduce Interference
note: The privacy-line scheme: what a privacy line buys (78), the hub-and-direction organisation (79-80), the direction categories and Figure 3's coloured network (81-82), and a worked routing example through repeaters 8 and 15 (83-84). Stored count 5 against four printed units.

heading: 4.5 K-Means Clustering (4.5.1 Connecting Clusters, 4.5.2 Assigning Channels)
note: The full algorithm: why clustering is needed and how k-means places repeaters (85-90), Algorithm 2 for network generation (91-103), the note that Cluster is plain k-means (104), the gap-closing distance measure (105-106), Algorithm 3 that connects components like a minimum spanning tree (107-118), channel assignment from the hub by closeness centrality (119-120), and Algorithm 4 walking outward one channel at a time (121-133). Stored count 8 against ten printed units.

heading: 5 Results (5.1-5.4)
note: The four result claims: repeater counts for the naive and clustered networks (135-138), coverage, where the naive method is 100 percent by construction and clustering loses a little (139-141), transmission capacity through simulation with its standard deviation at about one percent (142-144), and the share of requests processed (145-146). Tables 1-4 are single fragment groups. Stored count 8 against thirteen printed units.

heading: 6 Discussion (capacity and scaling)
note: How the model behaves as the load grows: the capacity improvement over the naive network (147), the scaling test at 10000 users (148-150), and the tenfold increase in network cost (151). Stored count 5 against four printed units.

heading: 6.1 Effects of hubs and 6.2 Effects of Mountainous Terrain
note: The two what-if analyses: localised hubs as a remedy for the single-hub weakness with Figure 5 (152-157), and mountainous terrain, where elevation both blocks line of sight and could reduce the repeater count (158-162). Stored count 10 against seven printed units.

heading: 7 Conclusion
note: Four concluding paragraphs: mountainous terrain could help rather than hurt (163), the algorithm does a good job overall (164), the cap on initial clusters limits it when the cluster count is wrong (165), and the behaviour when a good cluster count is supplied (166). Stored count 6 against four printed units.

heading: 8 Future Work (8.1 Limitations of our model, 8.2 Ways to improve the model)
